utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning to the technical booth; good morning to interpreters, the registry, the Prosecution and the Defence counsel. We shall resume our work, and it's Mr. Fila's turn to tell us what we are going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. president. The next witness will come in soon. I have planned four witnesses for today and another two for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the first for today is?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protected witness DC4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness DC4. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't quite hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Take your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Do you feel comfortable, Witness DC4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine. You will now be shown a piece of paper. There is a name written on it. You will tell us, yes or no, whether it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the moment, you will be answering questions asked of you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are moving into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Witness DC4, you said that you lived in Ljubija since 1956?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. 1956. Did you know Mladjo Radic known as Krkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He was a simple policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the national structure of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: It was mixed. It was entirely mixed, Croats, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What can you tell us about his conduct in that environment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: All the best. He was a simple policeman. He did his work. We were neighbours. He helped people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you notice in his conduct any nationalist attitude or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that a member of your family found himself detained at one stage in the investigations camp of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know why he found himself there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Well, because he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like you now to use your own words, without any further information -- intervention on my part, to explain about his stay in Omarska. He was there for about two months, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Two months or 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he meet there Mladjo Radic and what did he tell you about that meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: I heard that my brother was arrested because my son from Prijedor told me so, and I arrived because I knew him and his wife. I called them by phone. I asked whether it would be possible for me to bring medicines and food and some clothes. His wife answered that Mladjo will answer me and Mladjo said, "Yes, bring those things and, if I can, I'll bring them in." I started early. I set off early. There was no electricity. I got hold of those things and I gave another call to his wife and told that -- told her that Mladjo should pick them up. He did, and he brought those things to my relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Food, medicines, some clothing, like trousers, T shirts,. He took all those things. Then I went back home to Ljubija. Later, Mladjo dropped in. I asked him whether he would be able to take medicines to him, because he had an ulcer, a stomach ulcer, and he said, "I'll take these things, and if I can, I'll let him have them." It was not a big parcel. There was food, clothes, some money, those people received -- admitted all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Zenkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did -- was Mladjo Radic anything to him? Did he do anything for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes. He waited at my place. His wife was preparing food for him, and he took him the food, a leather jacket, 100 Deutschmarks, and his wife later told me that he had received all those things. And he brought things to other people as well. He said he would try to take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that permitted and was it easy to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't, because Mladjo was a simple policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you meet him after the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After the camp, what was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: As usual, he was an ordinary policeman. He was working in the SUP of Prijedor. I dropped in on a friend who was shift leader. Mladjo was at the reception desk. He saw me and greeted me. He was at the counter, a number 92. He was a simple policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your brother lived in Prijedor. He's not from Ljubija, is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, he lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Milomir Antunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: I can say that he was in the camp. He is from a village. And when Mladjo was doing his rounds while on duty in Ljubija, he visited him. He had a relative, Milicic Milka and when he visited him, he dropped in on her, and she asked him if he could do anything for Milomir, if he could help him get released, and he answered that that was difficult, that he could see what he can do, and see who is in charge. He said he would try through people who were responsible. And when he got out, Milomir got out, and he is now in Croatia, those who were responsible said that he had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you talk to your brother once he got out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He told me that he had received everything from Mladjo, that Mladjo had given him bread, the several parcels, and that Mladjo had also given him some cigarettes and that he was a good man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of some other people whom he had helped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Kubil Kosevic [phoen] -- Bilkic, sorry, and there were other people. I can't remember them all. Sefik, Antunovic, my brother, others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why wouldn't those people come here to testify, including your brother, or could they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Well, we don't dare because of their safety. He doesn't dare. He fears for his own safety. It's a different country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does he know that you're testifying? Did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, he knows everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything in connection with your coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He said, "Go ahead," because I sent all my parcels through Mladjo. And I'm testifying because I have personal knowledge and he told me himself that this was a good man who helped people as much as he could, hiding from others, doing it on the sly from people who were higher up Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did your brother evaluate the conduct of Mladjo Radic and how do you evaluate it? What do you think about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Great. He was a good and honest man always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, asking for an opinion from this witness with regard to another opinion given by another person. This is not hearsay but double hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, ask the witness what her brother had told her about the conduct of the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did your brother tell you about Mladjo's conduct? I'm sorry. I wanted to make this shorter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: How did he behave himself? He was honest. He helped him as much as he was able to. He brought the things that I had sent, he gave him cigarettes when he could. He told me all that when he came back from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask that we move into private session again, because I want to ask a question which requires it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any other Defence counsel who wish to ask any more questions? I see negative shakes of the head. Mr. Simic? No. So, Mr. Waidyaratne, the witness is now yours. Witness, you will now answer questions asked of you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness DC4 - I will call you by that, as you are a protected witness - your brother asked you to come and testify; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he cannot come and that I should go instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Don't tell me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He doesn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Don't tell me as to where he is now. I don't want to know the place. But is he living in Bosnia or is he in a third country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He's in a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He's in a third country. But he still fears to come and testify; is that correct? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes. And last year he visited me and he said that he did not dare come. He got his house back in Prijedor but he doesn't dare return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He didn't tell you as to why he fears, although he's living in a third country, as to why he fears to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Well, there are people who were there, who did those things, who arrested him in Prijedor, and he's afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. His fear to come and testify, is that the reason, because they are in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: They are in Prijedor, yes, and he's afraid to go. He's afraid of the Serbs, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your brother is in a third country, not in Prijedor now. From the time after he left --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, he's in a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you have a house in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: I had a house in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say that these matters were discussed in closed session and Mr. Waidyaratne is now talking about it in open session, and this jeopardises the identity of the witness, (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Waidyaratne, please take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I respectfully request that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that would be safer. Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, your brother, before he was arrested, he was still undergoing medication; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And they didn't -- the people who took them to the camp did not allow him to take his medicine; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was your brother involved in politics or was he a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many children did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know as to why he was not allowed to take his medicine when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He wasn't at home when he was arrested. He was at his sister-in-law's having lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was not given an opportunity to take his medicine anyway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, now, you said this simple policeman, Mr. Radic, came specially to collect the things that you wanted to send to your brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He came. Whether he came specially for that or whether he'd had other business because there were some of his wife's relatives living there, but he stopped by anyway. When I called in the evening, I didn't go in the morning. I said all that; I don't want to repeat it. I asked Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him and he said yes, he would if he could bring it in because of the other people that were there, so he would do his best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the money, did you give the money or he requested the money to be taken to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No. He didn't ask. He couldn't request this. I asked him to take it. I gave medicines, I gave some clothing, I gave him some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, why did you send money to the camp? There were no shops in the camp. Did anybody tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask Mr. Waidyaratne to read the transcript and tell us where he sees that she said that she asked the money to be sent. So Mr. Waidyaratne should ask did he send it -- no, did she send money for her brother. That would be the proper question and the right way of going about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you send money through Mr. Radic to your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No, I did not send money. I sent him food, trousers, T shirts. I've already said that, medicines. I did not send any money, cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please refrain from making comments. And Mr. Waidyaratne, please proceed. I think that it is quite normal for counsel to reorganise himself and take a few moments to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: At page 3, line 15, the witness mentions this. Therefore that's why I asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think he mentioned that it was the other, the president of the SDA who asked Radic to take 100 Deutschmarks and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, I stand corrected. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you knew Mr. Radic took money to the camp for the people who were detained there; is that correct? You got to know about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He took it and the woman sent a leather jacket too and some food and 100 German marks and Irfan Zenkovic received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now that we are dealing with Irfan, do you know where he is now? I don't want to know the place but do you know whether he's alive or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: He died last year, somewhere in a third country. His brother returned to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you're supposed to have spoken to your brother. Did your brother say as to what position Mr. Radic had in the camp, as to what he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: An ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, as to what he performed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: What else could he be -- could he have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, as to what functions or what he did in the camp. I know that he's a policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes. What could an ordinary policeman do with just eight years of schooling? What else could he do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did your brother say as to what function he did, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Ordinary ones. No, he didn't. No, he didn't do anything that would require a position of any kind. An ordinary policeman, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour. Witness, you knew Mr. Radic for quite a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you said that he was an ordinary policeman; is that correct? Isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: But during the time that your brother was in the camp, he in fact did extraordinary things which could not have been done by an ordinary policeman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Well, when the people who -- I don't know how to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you know in advance what I'm about to say. That is an assertion. Counsel is making an assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are mutually accusing each other. Mr. Waidyaratne, don't make an assertion with the question mark at the end, but ask a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know any other policemen who were in the camp who did help people in the camp, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't interested in that, just I knew about him through my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes my -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you know that Mladjo Radic worked in the Omarska camp whatever the work was that he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Because my son worked in Omarska at the petrol pump and he knew his wife. She worked in the kitchen. She was a cook. And my son contacted them and asked where Mladjo was working because, for a time, he worked at the police station as an ordinary policeman, police officer, when he left Ljubija, and then they moved over there to work. And that's how I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did you know or did you not know that your brother was in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, I did know. My son told me that from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That means that you contacted Mladjo Radic because your son knew his wife and learnt that he was working in Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Judge Fouad Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will have to call you Witness DC4. Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I hope you can help me understand a few things to the best of your knowledge. You said that your brother was not involved in politics, was not a member of SDA. To your knowledge, why were people like him arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Only men or women too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Women, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Women too. And then concerning your intervention to send him food and the medicine, you think Mr. -- was it thanks to an acquaintance between you and Mrs. Radic or was it because your brother knew Mr. Radic? Because he can't do it for everyone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Of course he couldn't, of the other Serbs, no. He did this because we knew each other from the 1970s. We were acquaintances and he said that he would do as much as he could, to the best of his ability, but of course he was afraid of his other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whether you say "we," it means you or your brother? Who was a friend of Radic? Were you a friend of the family or that you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Me. I was friendly with their family, with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I don't think this is a secret but your brother is living outside now, abroad, in a third country? And he's afraid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He's afraid to go back -- afraid of the Serbs, not of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why would he be afraid then to come and testify here for a Serb, to defend a Serb? Is he afraid of the Muslims too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Well, he's afraid of the Muslims and Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But is he -- I mean, he has no contact with Muslims. His house is in a Serb area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald? No questions? I have a few questions for you, Witness DC4. You said that the people received all the things, all the things that Radic brought. Do you remember saying that? Have we got some more technical problems or can you hear the interpretation? Can you hear me, Madam? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me repeat. You said, and I'm quoting your words, the people received all the things. And I suppose that they were the things that Radic brought. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you know that the people had received all the things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC4
utterances.text: Because they were mostly my neighbours, and we contacted each other, visited each other. And Irfan's wife told me that Irfan had received everything, and that is why he had asked for money, because he thought he would go -- leave Omarska and go further on. And he went to Manjaca, and that's why he asked for the money. And let me also say that an individual told me - and she was a woman there - that Mladjo took his wife to the doctor's to get some medicines for her so that she could take the medicines to the camp, because she was ill. And he took out these medicines in the name of his own wife, to take the medicines to another woman prisoner, woman detainee, who was otherwise a neighbour of theirs. So that's what she told me. She told me all about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness DC4, we have no further questions for you. We should like to thank you very much for coming and we wish you a safe return to your place of residence. Thank you very much, and the usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, who is the next witness? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We have summaries for the next two witnesses because they live outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As Mr. Christian Rohde doesn't like us to spend the Tribunal's money travelling left and right, I saw them for the first time here, so I wasn't able to take a statement from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon will be taking this witness, Your Honour, but he apparently is satisfied that we can proceed. So thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Thank you for coming. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, please proceed. There is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may we move into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet, Mr. Fila. Witness, would you have a look at the piece of paper to see if your name is inscribed on it. Give us a yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is your name; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know a person named Mladjo Radic before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did you meet him and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I met him in the '70s when he came to work to Ljubija as a young police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I apologise for interrupting, but looking at the transcript - and I think we can do this in open session - we need the date of the witness' birth. Which February were you born? We need the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says the year, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better to move into private session for a few moments, and so let us do so. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the interpreters. I saw Mr. Saxon on his feet. Was there a problem, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There was, but perhaps we should go into private session and I will explain the problem to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session. Sorry, we are not in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you met Mladjo Radic in the '70s, in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: He was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is Ljubija a multi-ethnic place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Which nationalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Gypsies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During his work, did you notice that Mr. Radic differentiated between the nationalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No. Quite the opposite. At that time the police -- the regime was different. You couldn't even look at a policeman in an unfriendly way. But he was a member of my generation. We were doing sports together, we socialised, we went out together. It seems to me that the way he was on duty, he was the same way off duty too. We would make jokes on account of the police, even on his account, whereas we couldn't do that with others. We made jokes at our own expense, at his expense, and there were no problems at all, not even during his work, nor during his time off. We would go to restaurants together, we would chase women, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Please try and speak a little more slowly. You were going very fast earlier on, but try and speak a little more slowly, because you're speaking the same language, whereas we have to rely on the interpreters. So I apologise, but could I please ask you to speak more slowly, which will facilitate the work of the interpreters. Thank you. Mr. Fila, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DC5, at one point you found yourself detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Omarska camp. I arrived there in early July from the Keraterm camp. When I came to the Omarska camp, we arrived there in two buses. The majority from my group were from Ljubija, because in those days, in that period, the population of Ljubija was brought to the Keraterm camp. And because we couldn't be accommodated, we couldn't -- didn't have time for -- they didn't have time for everybody to be interrogated at that camp, so they took us by bus to the Omarska camp. When we got to Omarska camp, they brought us out of the buses. They lined us up into two lines. They turned us towards a wall, and while we were waiting to come in, out of boredom or something, the guards who were standing behind us forced us to put our hands on the wall, to put three fingers on the wall. Who -- the people who couldn't do that very well got hit on their hands. Then we were told to go into a room. It was a kind of small room. As we heard, this was the administrative building's garage. There were 74 of us. There was no room for all of us to stand, never mind to lie down. I spent three days there until it was my turn to go in for questioning. And during those three days, we would go out, if needed. We would just go out to go to the -- to go to the bathroom, but there was no proper toilet. We would have to just go out on the grass. And there was also a water tap outside. Once also they took us to the cafeteria to have lunch, and then they brought us back to that room. On the third day, it was my turn to go in for questioning. These questionings were held above the room that we were in, in offices on an upper floor. During the questioning, we would hear screams, the sounds of things breaking, howling. I think that there was torture. I don't know who was doing it. And I believe that the reason why we were held in this room was a psychological one so that we would know what would be waiting for us up -- upstairs, but even besides that, I personally couldn't wait to go upstairs because I knew that I had to go through that, and once you went through that, you could go out to the pista, where we saw a large number of internees who were outside. They could move around freely.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you stop for a second now and then we will continue with that. How much time did you spend in Omarska overall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think about a month.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The guard who made you lean against the wall with the three fingers, do you know who these guards belonged to? What were they dressed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: There were different uniforms there. It was summer, so they were wearing a drab, olive-grey military shirts, some people were wearing blue shirts. Some people even had camouflage pants and then they would be wearing a civilian T-shirt with short sleeves. So I wasn't sure but I was sure that they belonged to the Serb army. I couldn't say the army. I mean, they were all Serbs. And then all the inmates were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell us now whether you met Mr. Radic at Omarska and tell us about all your encounters with him. Could you tell us that in your own words without my further interruption? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I think the first time that I heard about Mladjo Radic was on the second day when we were coming back from lunch. When the guards who were returning us, two or three guards, lined us up in the same way that they did when we came out of the buses, in two lines, and we had to be turned towards one side. They forced us to sit down with our legs close to our bodies and with our heads between our knees. Then they started to beat us on our back.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Please, could you drink some water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: They beat us everywhere. They jumped on us. We didn't see who it was who was beating us, nor did we know how much they were beating us. At one point, I heard that somebody mentioned a name, Krkan, and then a little bit after that, they told us to go inside the garage. They made us run in there like a stampede so that at the door, we ran into one another and then we had to go in slowly. Once inside, we commented that we know a person called Krkan from the place where we came from. There were different nicknames. I don't know where his nickname came from.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You said that somebody mentioned Krkan. In which context was this mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: One of the guards said, "Stop, let's stop. Krkan is coming."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Stop what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: The beating. Then they stopped beating us and then we went inside the garage. And then once inside the garage, we were talking whether this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was the same Krkan that we knew, because there were different nicknames. Somebody thought that this was a derogatory nickname, somebody didn't think so, but I think that Mladjo Radic that we called Krkan had this nickname because he liked to eat a lot and drink a lot. So then we used to say that he gorged himself. We didn't mean anything bad by it. And we don't know who it was that the nickname originated from. So when it was my turn for questioning, the guard took me upstairs. I came to the office where there were two elderly, older gentlemen. One of them was reading a newspaper, the other one was waiting to interrogate me. And it seemed to me that they were on shifts. One was resting and the other one was doing the interrogating. So then once he took my information, he started to read from a piece of paper, where all the things that I was charged against were noted, the reason why I was brought to the camp. The first charges that he mentioned, I couldn't give an affirmative response to and I couldn't confirm that it -- the things happened that they ascribed to me. He laughed, and I said that this wasn't true and then I received a blow on my back. And until that moment, I didn't even realise that somebody was standing behind me. There was a young man there, also wearing a black T-shirt and camouflage trousers. When I -- I fell down off the chair and he hit me once again, and then I got up in order that he shouldn't hit me again. But, really, I didn't see him. Once I sat down again, then after a series of questions, after I denied all the things that were being ascribed to me, he came around to in front of me and he kicked me in the chest. And then I said for him not to touch me anymore. And then they asked me another couple of questions, and after that, they allowed me to leave and go to the pista. When I was coming out through the corridor, and I know I could -- I know that in front of every office I could hear that people were being beaten. I was walking ahead slowly. I was prepared to receive blows. But when I was in front of the last office, I could see that the guards who were usually in the offices, that the guards were sitting there and they were drinking coffee so that when I passed by there, nobody touched me. Only downstairs, there was one guard at the bottom of the stairs, and he was talking with this woman. He moved, and she thrust her foot out so that I stumbled and fell. I then went into the restaurant because the restaurant was there, the canteen was there. And I went inside because it was time for lunch, which lasted for two or three minutes, just enough time to eat the food. Then I went to the pista and I was amongst the other inmates who were there before me. There, I met other acquaintances who arrived at the camp before me and who were already outside at the pista. And then we talked. We didn't pay much attention to our surroundings, the day went by. I was asking, "How do things run here? How do they work?" And they said, "Well, you can go and have water. Most of the day you spend sitting around and then in the evening you go to these rooms where you spend the night." The first night at the pista, the first day, we spent there until dusk, until it was time to go to bed. They lined us up in groups of about 30 and they took us to the different rooms. I, in the group that I was in, went into one of the offices on the floor above. Later I saw that there was a large hole underneath that room where there was a large workshop. And then, in the course of the night, the guards would come in. Some of them would hit us, some of them would walk all over us, and they were asking for money and watches. It was very popular to see who was wearing these special sports shoes on their feet. So that practically we couldn't really spend the night -- we couldn't sleep during the night. In the morning they would take us out to the pista again where we would be lying around or sitting around all day. In the morning, when there was a committee that came around, we had to lie on our stomach so that we wouldn't see who the members of that committee were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you met -- when you encountered Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I met Mladjo Radic, I think, on the third day because I spent two nights upstairs on the upper floor. At one point, I looked and I saw a familiar face, because all of the guards were not known to me. And later I found out that all the guards were from the surrounding villages. The only person that I did recognise was him. I was thinking - and I was not sure - I was hesitating whether I should go up to him, for him to see me or that whether I should ask for help from him. I was afraid to approach him at first because I had friends, acquaintances, that I grew up with and who had forgotten me overnight. And they didn't know me any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Those were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I took a bottle from a friend of mine, that was -- it was a plastic bottle. The first guard who was there, usually you would ask the first guard for permission to go and get water, and he permitted me to go and get water. On the way back, I met -- I glanced at Mladjo Radic, and he looked at me and he was surprised, and he asked me when did I get there? And I said, "I got here two or three days ago, three or four days ago." He asked me, "Are there any problems?" And so on. And I asked him if it was possible for him to do something, to transfer us, so that we could sleep in the restaurant, with the groups who were in the restaurant, because usually that group had -- was a little more privileged. When we were taken out early in the morning, then you could get a place by the wall in the hall because that place had the most hours in the shade during the day. And he said that he would see with his colleague, the guard, who allocated which group would go where and he did go. So when it was time -- I didn't see him -- then I didn't see him any more. When it was time to go to sleep, the guard who was allocating the groups, he said right away the group from Ljubija should line up there. There were a lot of us from Ljubija but there were a few groups of 30. We lined up. We waited for other groups to line up, five or six more lines. That is how many windows there were to go into the restaurant, because that was the way we went into the restaurant, through low windows, which were set quite low. So among the first, we entered the restaurant and then the other groups, that's where we spent the night. And we were a little protected there. It wasn't quite peaceful but nobody really touched us there. Perhaps somebody would come and call somebody out and take them out. This went on, repeated itself for two or three more days, as far as going inside the restaurant. Then when he was in the shift, there was an outbreak of dysentery. There were some stomach problems. He would bring us medicines. He would bring us some pills. And people were helped by those pills.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic. Once, at one point, he passed me a small piece of bread when lunch was already over, just in passing, so that I should have that piece of bread, and I divided it between the two or three of us. Later I heard from other people that he would pass them bread too, in passing. I was -- I spent most of my time among people from Ljubija, and two or three days later we were transferred. We were not to sleep any longer down in the pista. We were moved into a hall which was cleared for inmates. When we arrived at the hall, three big doors were opened. Those doors were usually used by dumper trucks and when we got there we noticed that it was partitioned by a barbed wire about one metre high and that the hall had been washed, the floor had been washed. It was still wet. It was still wet with oil and dust. There was a layer of dirt actually on the floor. They made us lie down and get up several times and used us to sweep the floor with our bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you meet Mladjo Radic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I met him again on that same day, sometime in the afternoon, when he brought two or three loaves of bread, but I didn't get it then. My colleagues -- in fact, my friends, comrade inmates got it, those who were nearer to the wire. The next day also he brought some bread for me but that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. towards the evening. He called me out by name to come close to the wire, and he brought a paper bag containing 20 fourths of bread. Usually we would get just one eighth of a loaf of bread for dinner. So he gave us this paper bag full of bread, and to divide between us. Later, I was called by a guard who was on duty, and he told me to bring that bag over to him. When I did so, he took two fourths of bread out of the bag, and he said, "You can have the rest, and I'm taking this for my pigs because they are worth more than you are." And when Radic heard of that, he said, "Don't tell Radic this, because darkness will swallow you." I never told Radic, because I knew what the expression meant. They had little respect for us, those other guards. But he defended us and we were somehow under his protection. And the bread that was taken away from me, I believe it was out of some sort of spite. He wanted to prove to me that he can go against Radic even.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Regarding the shifts, did you have any particular name for that shift where Mladjo Radic worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: When I arrived at the camp, I heard from my acquaintances that there were shifts there, and although I didn't know who did what duties, I didn't distinguish between the uniforms. But among us, we referred to it as Mladjo's shift. In fact, we used the word "Krkan's shift," because he was on it. And there were really -- there were a couple of guards on it who - I don't know how to put it - had absolutely no human feeling. It didn't take them anything to beat a man up. For instance, we were mostly beaten by those who were in the compound, within the hall, and I never saw Mladjo Radic around there. They had no particular designated guard posts. They just walked around the hall.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What did he carry in terms of weapons, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him ever with a weapon. The first time I saw a weapon on him was when I had got out of the camp and when I was in Croatia, and then I saw him on TV carrying an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was that a film?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a brief, short landing on a staircase. You could see through the rails. And he was standing there with an automatic rifle. And there were many other guards without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Why did you call it Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Because he was the only one we knew on that shift.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How would you evaluate his conduct, his treatment of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I can understand -- I could understand if Mladjo Radic wanted to protect me, because he knew me, but there were 30 other people who enjoyed the same protection as I did, and we would have been much luckier if dear God had wanted us to have several more other guards in that camp who would have taken another 20 or 30 people under their protection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the counsel. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You left to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone. Mr. Fila has no microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you go to Manjaca from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you meet other inmates who had been in Omarska with you and did you then make any comments among yourselves about Mladjo Radic? Did you discuss him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: A part of the inmates also from Ljubija who had been with me, they were called out again on the pista, and it later turned out that those people who had been called out left for the camp in Trnopolje and had been returned home from there. We were told that all the others who had not been called out to get onto buses. Seventeen buses or thereabouts had arrived to take us to Manjaca. In Manjaca we had a bad time in the first days as well. There were guards. We couldn't talk much. They made us keep our hands behind our backs. But several days later, the Red Cross came and registered us and things improved; they improved a lot. Living conditions were better, we were able to move around, we were able to move from the stable, where we were accommodated, we could talk to other inmates. And in our discussions we sort of reviewed our memories, and as far as Mladjo Radic is concerned, nobody ever mentioned seeing him hit somebody or anything worse than that. All I could hear in my group -- I cannot speak about other people, but in my group of 30 or 50 people who were in Manjaca from Ljubija, that's all you could hear about him, and I speak in my name only. I have gone through hell, but in that hell, I enjoyed only one protection, and that was Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you very much for all the good things that you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. I think that we're going to take a break at this point. Before we take a break, I should like to ask the usher to escort you, Witness, out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Are there any other Defence counsel who wish to put questions to this witness? All right. Very well. Thank you. Mr. Saxon -- witness, you are now going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For my first two questions, could we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are moving into private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was: Did you and Mr. Radic go to restaurants together and chase women until 1984, when Mr. Radic was transferred to the Omarska Police Department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No. When Mr. Radic left Ljubija, we saw less of each other. For some time I worked in Ljubija. After that I worked in Prijedor. I actively engaged in sports and I had less time to spare and we saw less of each other in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, DC5, perhaps my question wasn't clear. I'll try to ask it again. My question was: Did you and Mr. Radic continue to go to restaurants together, chase women together, from the 1970s until 1984, which was when Mr. Omarska was transferred -- Mr. Radic was transferred to the Omarska Police Station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We did go out together but it was not very frequently. From time to time, we would go out in other surrounding towns. Would I sometimes go out after work and so did he. He had a small car, a Fiat 750, and he -- I had a wife and he had a girlfriend, a stable girlfriend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic have a stable girlfriend in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: She wasn't exactly from Ljubija but later when he got married, it's a small place near Ljubija, it's his present wife. At that time, I didn't see them go out together very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After you and Mr. Radic were married in the mid 1970s, did you continue to go out together and chase women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We would meet in places, cafes, where we went out, both of us, where people from Ljubija met but we no longer went out and had fun as bachelors. I already said that I was employed at the time. I was also a sportsman. I went -- I was busy doing my training and preparations and we would meet by chance somewhere when we went out for a drink and we made jokes and hoaxes together, because he was very good at that, and that was the sort of fun we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's move to the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's move to your detention in the Omarska camp in July of 1992. You mentioned an incident -- actually, I need to go more slowly. In your direct examination, you were asked about the guards at the Omarska camp. This was on page 29 of the transcript. And you said that there were different uniforms there but you were sure that they belonged to the Serb army. My question is: Is it possible that these men who were wearing different kinds of clothing were actually reserve policemen who had been mobilised to serve as guards at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I do not know that. What I could see at the camp looked to me as a poorly organised army, very loose, because not only did they wear a variety of uniforms and black T-shirts - those black T-shirts were worn by bigger men who probably wanted to show off their muscles - and some of them wore drab-olive shirts, some wore grey-olive shirts, others wore blue police shirts. So it was really a great variety of clothing and you couldn't distinguish between ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident where a beating of prisoners was going on that you witnessed, and you heard a guard say, "Stop. Let's stop. Krkan is coming." When that guard uttered those words, did the beating stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I only heard somebody say, "Stop." I don't know whether they said, "Krkan is coming." I didn't even see him then. I didn't see from which side somebody was coming. There was a car coming - we could hear that - but the car was far away, and it was ten minutes through the beating. Maybe they had got tired of it themselves. I don't know the meaning of all this. I didn't know. It was Mladjo Radic in question. But as it later turned out, it was he who was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On page 30 of the transcript, at line 9, Witness DC5, your words were: "One of the guards said, 'Stop. Let's stop. Krkan is coming.'" My question was, and please just answer yes or no: After you heard those words, did the beating stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not right away, but they said, "Away with you. Go to the garage."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After that, did Krkan, the man you knew as Mladjo Radic, arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We did not see him, because they had already marched us into the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So as far as your personal knowledge, you heard these words uttered by the guard and after that the beating stopped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned how, and I think also with the assistance of Mr. Radic, you and other prisoners from Ljubija were permitted to sleep in the restaurant. And on page 34, this is what you said. You said: "So we were a little protected in the restaurant." By the pronoun "we," are you referring to yourself and your neighbours from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes. That means me and the people in my group there, because when I went to ask after -- when I went to ask him, I asked for myself and the people who were with me. I didn't know any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC5, you mentioned that there was an outbreak of dysentery at the camp, some prisoners had stomach problems. Do you know what was making the prisoners ill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Probably poor nutrition. I don't know what. I'm not a doctor. I can't say that. All I know is that we asked something to be done to stop this dysentery or alleviate it a little. There was one doctor among the inmates who provided medicines as well, and when he was not there, then we asked Mladen to bring something in. I personally did not need any, but I know that some inmates who were with me had in their possession a couple of pills received from the doctor who was one of the inmates, some of them had pills they got from Mladjo Radic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC5, you described a scene where one of the guards took some bread from the prisoners who were in your group - I believe you were in the hangar - and the guard said to you and your fellow prisoners, "You can have the rest and I'm taking this for my pigs, because they are worth more than you are." This is on page 35 of the transcript of your direct testimony. But in the English translation, according to the English translation, you continued to say: "And when Radic heard of that, he said," and then it says, "Don't tell Radic this, because darkness will swallow you." I'm concerned, first of all, there may be some confusion in the translation. Who was it who made that last comment, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I didn't say that Radic said that. I said that the guard who had taken away some bread from my bag -- there were several guards there around the dumper gates, and they sat at desks. One of those guards, he took two fourths of bread out of the bag and he said: Have the rest and I'll take this for his pigs. And he said, "If I tell Radic about that, darkness would swallow me."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, or in your opinion, what did that guard mean by that comment?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The guard took everything but two fourths of the loaf.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We, the group from Ljubija, consisted of about a hundred men, but in that hangar there were 30 of us. And when he would bring bread or medicines, he communicated through me, because I was the one he knew best, and I divided whatever I received with the rest of the people. He was our protection of some kind, and the others must have known it. I don't know why this man took away the bread that Radic had brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You described a couple of guards on Krkan's shift as people with "no human feeling," and you said, "It didn't take them anything to beat a man up." What were the names of these guards that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I didn't know. All I knew that these were guards from the surrounding villages, villages around Omarska, and I assume they lived there because when the gates were open, when we were lying on the pista, we saw them coming to their -- to work on bicycles but I didn't know any of them personally. I knew them by sight, but I didn't know anyone by name from that area because I came from another region, and before that, I had never been -- I hadn't been to Omarska very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did Mr. Radic do about the behaviour of these guards who had, as you put it, no human feeling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't know because I didn't see it. I was in that hall, that hangar. Our movement was restricted. We could only go to the toilet, and sometimes they opened the doors for us to sit by the entrance where the bars were outside and I couldn't overhear their conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Witness DC5, that the origin of the term "Krkan's shift" amongst the prisoners at the Omarska camp actually came from the brutal behaviour of these inhumane guards who served with Mr. Radic on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Those individual guards on that shift were brutal but we - especially we the people from Ljubija - called it "Krkan's shift" because he was on it and we watched out for his shift because we expected from him some protection, some freedom of movement, and we could also expect to get some of those things we needed, medicines, food, and we looked forward to his shift so we could get some of those things we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "we," you're referring to the 30 other people from Ljubija who you mentioned, who enjoyed the same protection as you did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, were these 30 people and yourself beaten by these brutal guards who didn't have any human feeling or were they protected successfully by Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: The people who were beaten, when they were beaten in the hall, then nobody knew who was doing the beating and what was happening because it was done in the dark. When we were lying down, one across the other, one over the other, because there were so many people of us there, they would stamp and walk all over us, so we didn't know who was doing that. However, the fact that none of us people from Ljubija were called out during the night, except some perhaps who were on some lists or something like that -- I don't actually know whether they were requested by someone from outside or how those lists were compiled, but I think that it did have an effect. That is to say, the guards bypassed us, if I can put it that way, compared to the other people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: They bypassed you except when they weren't beating you and the prisoners in that group; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Your Honour, I see Mr. Fila shaking his head. I heard the word "nay" coming from that direction. This is a court of law and we have to be careful, I believe, that what the court hears is the witness's own testimony, not any kind of coached version of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. President, I did not say a single word. I did not utter a single word. I was nodding my head and looking at Mr. Saxon because there was a mistake in the interpretation. And if you come here to my seat, you can see that I can't see the witness at all from where I'm sitting. Secondly, all my years of service, you know, I do not use tricks like that. Perhaps they exist in America, but in Yugoslavia where I come from, I don't use tricks of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, I did not hear any words. I did not observe what happened. But we have Mr. Fila's word and we have what you said. It is true that we know [In English] pictures speak louder than words. [interpretation] And so verbal communication is stronger. I -- that is to say, pictures are stronger. I myself did not hear but maybe you have reason to think what you think. Anyway, let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC3 -- excuse me, DC5, you mentioned that you spent a number of nights sleeping in the restaurant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also just testified that no -- no one from Ljubija was called out at night except perhaps for some people who were on lists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I understand your testimony, you said that Mr. Radic communicated through you because "I was the one that he knew best." Does that mean that he, Mr. Radic, communicated through you to other prisoners from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: When he would bring me some bread or anything else, he would call me to hand it over to me, to give me the bread for me to distribute it amongst the others. And when we were on the pista, I would see others -- not when I was shut up in the hall but on the pista. When I was on the pista, when we were allowed to get up a bit, then I could see him move around many of the detainees and talk to them, whereas the other guards didn't even enter the -- that mass of people, mass of detainees who were out there on the pista, lying down, standing up or sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you were in the restaurant at night and Mr. Radic wanted to communicate in some way with the prisoners from Ljubija, would he communicate through you? Would he call you out of the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: When we were in the restaurant, he never -- nobody called us after that. It was the -- we were -- received the order to lie down and go to sleep and then early on in the morning, at 5.00 a.m. we would go out on to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before the war, -- before the war, in 1992, did you know a man from the town of Ljubija named Ismet Taras?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Ismet Taras? I think his surname was Taras and if it's the same person, Ismet Taras, he was also a policeman in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ismet Taras was also detained at the Omarska camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I didn't see him but I heard one night, when they came to look for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell me what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I was in the restaurant at that time. Three or four guards turned up. We were lying down and not looking who they were. They just asked, "Is Ismet Taras here?" And they repeated that two or three times. And when I responded, they went out and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So in other words people did come to the restaurant at night to call prisoners out. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here is what one former detainee from Omarska said about you and Ismet Taras: "One night around the 10th of July, you tried to call Ismet Taras out of the crowded restaurant" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't understand. One witness happened to say somewhere something, perhaps somewhere privately, with Mr. Saxon, while I was not in -- we should like to know which witness, when did he say that, and where was he when he said that. What did he mean that a man said something sometime somewhere? What does that mean? Was it like that or was it not? I don't know. And it is not customary to tell one witness what another witness said, according to the rules of procedure of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I respond to that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Fila is concerned about hearsay, well, the prior witness to this witness spent half an hour here giving hearsay evidence, so obviously that is a common occurrence, not only in this courtroom, but also in this Tribunal. Rule 90(H)(2) -- Your Honour, may I continue? Rule 90(H)(2) says that: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by that witness." Now, according to the Rule, I have to put my case to this witness. I have to put the Prosecution's case to this witness. If the Prosecution has information that suggests that this -- that the evidence given by -- that contradicts the evidence given by this witness, and it's relevant to the Prosecution's case, under the Rules, I have to be able to put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to give the floor to Mr. Fila, but before I do so, I do not think that that was the point that Mr. Fila raised. What Mr. Fila said -- he didn't say that you don't have the right to say what you said. All he asked was who the witness was and where you took the quotation from. Is that right, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise, Mr. President. That is precisely what I was going to say. If it is Mr. Saxon's testimony, perhaps he is a witness in this trial, and then I heard it and that's all right. Perhaps he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, could you tell us the name of the witness or the page of the transcript, and we shall resolve the issue straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is a person who has given information to the Prosecution, Your Honour. If I'm going to give the name of the witness, I'd like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move into private session, let's hear Mr. Fila. You wish to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, that witness' name was not disclosed previously, which means that something is kept back from us, because we have no idea about it. So you cannot use something that you say was said to you, to somebody from the Prosecution. How do I know what you say to each other? But that is irrelevant for me. And second, your time was up a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true. The second point is true. Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question. Why is Mr. Saxon nodding his ahead now? I don't understand what that nodding means. And you don't permit me to nod my head, so why should he be allowed to nod his head? Why is he nodding now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are entering into a dangerous field now, so let us proceed with caution. Let us move into private session to give Mr. Saxon a chance to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The name that was mentioned -- don't repeat the name, but the name that was mentioned, do you know that man by that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I think I do, from Ljubija, but -- I knew all the people from Ljubija and they knew me, but I didn't know all their names. (redacted) (redacted). I think it is a younger man. There were several people with that same surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon. You were going to say that the name was uttered; is that right? We shall have it deleted

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila says that he did not mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you spoke about the fact that Krkan in some way protected the people of Ljubija, did that refer to 30 of them or to more people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there were that many people from Ljubija at that particular place at that time, but I heard from detainees earlier on who were from Ljubija and who knew -- I didn't contact the people I didn't know because there were many detainees from around Prijedor, and I would go into the group that I knew, of the people I knew, and nobody ever said that Mladjo took anybody out to be beaten or that he saw him beat any anyone or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And my last question for you, Witness DC5, do you know whether Mladjo Radic, nicknamed Krkan, was superior to the man who took the bread away from you? Was he superior to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Of course not. I really don't -- couldn't say that anybody was superior to anybody else. It was such a mixture, everybody did what they pleased. There was no discipline whatsoever amongst the guards. So that I cannot say that he was superior in any way to anybody or the function and post he held. I know that of the higher up people that came, if anybody came that was higher up, they would come -- they would go to the offices up there. And if anybody higher up would come, we would have to lie down face downwards on the pista, not to see who was coming from the commission, from a committee of any kind or from commanders of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that nobody issued orders for somebody to beat you or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No. It was at random. When they were feeling bored, they would just lash out at you for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, witness, I can't say your name. Could you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
