utterances.text: Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like your opinion or your explanation for certain things you said. You mentioned that the guards bypassed your group, the 30 people from Ljubija. If you compare them to the other people, you were more or less exempted from beatings or torture or -- and so on. Did you notice other groups, too, which were privileged like your group and who were treated with more kindness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice groups. Perhaps some individuals who had contact. I would see them speaking with a guard. I don't know what they would be talking about, whether it was something private or something official. But like I said, if there had been more guards like Mladjo Radic so that they could protect a group, I think that that would make a good number of protected people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you mean Radic could only -- cannot extend his protection to everyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what his options were, what he could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in the two instances you mentioned that you said Krkan - you mentioned him under the name of Krkan - that he was considered by the people who were beating, one of them, which you said twice, when one of the guards said, "Let us stop beating, Krkan is coming." And you explained that the Prosecutor and to the Defence counsel. I will not go back to it. And then another case, the case concerning the bread, I think, when he took the bread to give to the pigs, "I told you -- don't tell Radic -- don't tell Radic that because darkness will swallow you" and so on. And also you said there was no difference whatsoever among the guards. What in your opinion made them take Radic's presence in consideration and have this kind of respect for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't know. Thinking about it now, I wouldn't say it was any kind of respect. First of all, I would say that it was more going against him because Radic was helping a few of the inmates, people who were not of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, was it against him, for instance, that you were more or less privileged, the people from Ljubija, and you were not beaten like the others, as you said? That was almost a privilege and some kind of respect for the people whom he was a friend of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I think that it was that mostly. People are not all the same. They don't have the same feelings. And also what I said at the beginning, I grew up with a lot of those people. We would go out together for years, have fun. We would play together. But the majority of them forgot me overnight. But in my case, this didn't happen as far as Radic was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But this privilege was not only extended to you? It was extended to all the people from Ljubija, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes. That group. We got together as a group on our own initiative because we were from Ljubija. We knew one another. We would help one another if somebody didn't feel too well. Other groups did that too. Muslims were in their own group, depending on which area they were from, so that's what we did. We made up our own group from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But what you called Radic -- what you called "Krkan's shift" did not hurt this group as a whole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This group was not badly treated by what you called "Krkan's shift" or by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, individuals did act. You couldn't really choose your place. If you walked by, the guard would hit you, regardless of whether something was your fault or not. This was especially done after the cleaning of the bathrooms, after the bathrooms were cleaned. It was a sort of entertainment for the guards to wait for two or three inmates and to beat them. This was just something that individuals did. It was a kind of abuse carried out by individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps what you said before, that when it was in the dark or somebody, there was no distinction, and nobody could distinguish who is who. But when you were together, the people from Ljubija, were you subject to mistreatment or were you treated better than the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No. Anyway, during the day, there wasn't so much mistreatment. During the day, we were not really touched in the hall. Only if you went to get water, for example, or went to the toilet, then a guard would either hit you or do something like that. At night, they used to come in and they would ask for money, watches, valuables. Then they would sort of search us. They would thrust their hands into our pockets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also to the group -- to your group in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We were in a group all mixed up together, so to tell you the truth, one of the inmates was in the hall, who, how can I put it, was used by certain guards and he did that work for them. He would walk amongst us and then, during the day, he would know whether any of us had money or cigarettes or cookies, and then during the day they would see that. And then at night, he would work for those guards, he would collect the money or whatever we had, so that that particular inmate -- I know that his own people beat him up at Manjaca because he left with us together for Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You said at one point in your testimony that after you had been at Omarska a couple of days, you knew that all guards were -- all the guards, you said, were from surrounding villages. Those are the words that I took down. Did you mean by that all the guards were policemen, reservists from the surrounding villages, or all the guards, some were reservists and some were army people from surrounding villages? Were you able to distinguish between those guards who were policemen like Mr. Radic, reservists and those guards who were members of some kind of army unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I didn't say -- maybe I said -- maybe I said I knew, but I just assumed that those soldiers or guards were from the neighbouring area. There were a lot of Muslims where whose villages bordered with these other villages so that they knew these people better, so that -- they knew there were hills around the camp so that they know that some guard would come from there, somebody would walk to work, somebody would come on a bicycle, so it was assumed that they would come to the shift from their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I'm more interested in whether or not you were able to tell whether the guards were from the police in the local villages, like Omarska, or whether they were from a mobilised army unit. Were you able to tell, make that distinction, whether the guards were policemen, former policemen, or policemen like Mr. Radic or whether they were part of an army unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't say. There were different uniforms really so I really don't know. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did the police like Mr. Radic wear uniforms that were different from the people who were in army units? Or were they all mixed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: They were completely mixed. Some people were in blue police shirts. Next to him would be another soldier who would be wearing an olive-grey shirt. Then there were others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. At the time that you were being beaten, when one of the guards said, "Krkan's coming" and they let you people go back into your rooms, could you tell then whether or not the ones who were beating you were soldiers or policemen guards? Just were you able to tell whether they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I couldn't because after that lunch, when we had to run outside with our heads bent, our head was always bent down, and then we were told to crouch down and so when we were beaten, these people were behind us, so we never knew who it was who was beating us. And a lot of time has passed so I can't really remember anything much about the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you were recounting the story of the guard that took the bread from you, in two different places the translation came through to me differently, and I just want to get it straight from you, whether or not what the guard said was, "If you tell Krkan, darkness will swallow me," or was it, "If you tell Krkan, darkness will swallow you"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: "Darkness will swallow you," meaning me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, but it came across differently twice. My last question is: While were you there, who did you think was in charge of the camp? I mean, did you think there was any head man in the camp? You talked about the guards being -- having no discipline and doing a lot what they wanted to, but was it yours and the other detainees' impressions, who shared those impressions with you, that anybody was in charge? I mean, was there anybody at the head of this camp? Were there any people who had some more power over how the camp ran than other people? I mean, it would be very difficult to have a camp with 6.000 people in it in which nobody was in charge. What was your impression of how the camp was run?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't know. To tell you the truth, I wasn't really interested that much. I was only looking to survive it all. What we could see, whether there were any commanders, any familiar faces, when they would come to the camp, we had to lie down on our stomachs with our heads covered so that we wouldn't see those people who would be coming there in the shift or who would be going to the administrative building, so I don't know what the schedule was. I know that it wasn't really strictly so that a guard would be standing in one fixed spot with a rifle. No. They would be walking around generally throughout the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you have told us that you did feel more protected, a little bit more protected, when Mr. Radic's shift was there. You felt you had some kind of a friend or a protector? That's what you said, I think, very directly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were there any --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there anybody else among the guards that you or other detainees that you knew of felt that way about, felt that they had a little more protection when that particular person was on the spot? Was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I just concentrated on Krkan and I did have the sense that he would help me after our first meeting when he saw me. I know that he said the first time that he would see, with his colleague, the one who was doing the allocating, if he could perhaps switch us, transfer us to the restaurant. And perhaps the other guards saw that we often talked with him and that he would approach us, so perhaps that's why they didn't abuse us so much. Perhaps because it could have been some other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness, on several occasions you mentioned the fact that not to see the committee or the commanders or anybody else in higher authority, you had to lie down, face downwards, on the pista. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know that that was so? How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: We knew more or less when the committee would come in the morning. They would come in a small mini van. We could see it coming from far off. And then we would be issued with the order, "Lie down on your stomachs and put your heads down." Then we would be ordered to get up again when the committee went inside the offices, upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What led you to conclude that you were ordered to do so so as not to see those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, as soon -- I don't know if it was an order, but we would be sitting around or standing, and then we would be told, "Lie down on your stomachs and heads down," and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just that? They didn't say "Lie down with your heads down" so that you should not be able to see the people? They didn't give that additional explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it is from this order and what followed the order, you were able to conclude that you were ordered to do so, to lie down, so as not to be able to see the people passing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever see the people? Did your curiosity not lead you to have a peep at the people? Did you ever see one or more of those people who were coming in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: Well, no, it didn't. Fear was greater. I couldn't raise my head, out of fear. I didn't do so personally. I don't know if any other people did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how did you know that those people were commanders or members of this committee or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC5
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were commanders, but I knew that they were members of the interrogation committee. I knew that from talking with the inmates, because they would come at a certain fixed time and they would leave at a certain fixed time, as if they had set working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. We have no further questions for you, Witness DC5. We should like to thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal and we wish you a good return back to your place of residence. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and I would just like to say goodbye to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, as you see, non-verbal communication is also a strong form of communication, and I understood, without you having to say anything, that this witness would be very brief and that we would get through him before the lunch break. Was I correct in my assumption? You didn't say anything, but I understood everything through our non-verbal communication. Who is the next witness? DC6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DC6. It's also a witness that we didn't have a chance to see up until yesterday. He lives outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Susan Somers, do you have any comments to make, any objections to make with respect to the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that if any type of summary, even a brief one, is available moments before the witness testifies, that it be provided to the Prosecution. I think that would be appropriate. And it is my understanding Mr. Saxon will be able to proceed. However, I am concerned inasmuch as we are held to the same standard of providing whatever we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I believe that we know the principle, but it was not always a rule from the viewpoint of the Prosecution. But I believe that Mr. Fila has explained the principle now. I believe he will do it as soon as possible. Very well. Yes, please have the witness ushered in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration that has been given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Make yourself as comfortable as you can. Thank you very much for having come here. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Yes, thank you, Mr. Fila. You will now be shown a piece of paper which has your name written on it. You will confirm, yes or no, if it is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to go briefly into private session for the sake of the particulars of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are moving into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, did you know a person named Mladjo Radic before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did you come to know him and how well do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I have known him since 1977, when I moved to that place. We met at the police station, because my military service consisted of doing a turn in the reserve police. We were attached to the reserve -- to the police station as assistants, and we conducted patrols in surrounding villages and towns, we did inspections and checks. We also met in the hunting club, where we were both members and through which we went hunting together with more of our friends who were with us, and those friends were of various ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At that time, what could you tell us about the attitude of Mladjo Radic to other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: He did not discriminate among nationalities. In our group of hunters there were three Muslims, including myself, several Croats, and the others were Serbs. I don't know exactly how many of us there were. Two of us Muslims were doctors.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Until what time were you in the reserve force of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Until the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What were you told then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina I was serving on the reserve police force for quite a while. Perhaps two or three months I didn't go to work to my company as usual, but I was helping out on the reserve police force. And on the 4th of June, 1992, that morning our commander was allocating assignments and he asked me to stay behind in his office because he had something to tell me. I did indeed stay behind, and he said, "I'm sorry, but you will have to be relieved of your duties today." At that moment I had on me a pistol that was issued to me as a reserve policeman. He told me that I should go home and bring back the other things that I was issued with: a uniform and other weapons. That was an automatic rifle. I did go home then and returned to the police station and returned all those things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DC6, we will now turn our attention to the day when you were arrested. And will you please tell us, where were you taken and who did you see in that place where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: On the 21st of July, at 8.00 in the morning, since there is no doorbell in the apartment where I resided - I was still sleeping - they knocked -- somebody knocked on the door, I got up and opened it. There were two policemen there, both of whom I knew. One was a reserve policeman, another was an active-duty policeman. They told me I was to go to the police station with them to give some sort of statement. I thought it had to do something with my returning the uniform and the weapons I had been issued with. I was aware that I hadn't signed any document to certify that I had returned them, so I said, "Okay. No problem. I'll be right back. Just let me dress." They said, "No, no, no. Don't. You don't need anything, no clothing, nothing. You just come with us." So I put on my shirt. They had a van outside. They put me in the van and took me to the police station. I entered, but there was no interview with anyone. I thought there would be an interview with a superior of some kind, but they just put me in a chair and told me to wait. I waited for about half an hour. Then another policeman came and told me to -- that I should go downstairs with him, because at that time we were on the upper floor. We went outside the building. There was a van and he told me to enter from behind. Inside there were two other guys whom I didn't know. They were younger men, 20-ish. And I asked them, "Where are we going?" He told me, "I don't know." And I said, "Will you please pass by my apartment so that I can take my jacket or something warmer. It's so cold outside." He said, "Okay. No problem." But when we were passing by the building where I lived, he simply rushed by without stopping. It was rather suspicious to me. I didn't know where we were going. I know the roads there, and I know he took the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and he drove me to Omarska. When we entered through the gate, he drove me to some kind of building, a house. We left the van -- we were in the van. There was one active-duty policeman escorting us and the reserve policeman was behind the wheel. When we arrived, Mladjo Radic came. I didn't see him coming. And he said, "How come you're here?" And I said, "I don't know. They just picked me up this morning, without any explanation." And then he asked this escort, this policeman, he asked him why I was brought, and the other man answered that he didn't know. He showed him some papers and he said, "Let me see those papers. I'll go and check. It must be a mistake of some kind." And he left with those papers in his hand. In the meantime, another man came wearing a camouflage uniform and ordered us out of the van. He took us inside, into the hallway, and ordered us to face the wall, raise our arms and put our hands on the wall, and then he frisked us. He asked us whether we had any weapons or anything. He searched us, but he was rather crude. He called us -- he cursed us and yelled. But when Mladjo Radic came back, he brought the papers and he said to the driver that we should be driven back to Ljubija, that it was all a mistake and that we shouldn't be there. So we were put back into the van and they took us away. I thought we were driving toward my home. They stopped in Prijedor, in a side street behind the department store, and they said they were going to the Prijedor Police Station to ask what to do next. But since I know well where the police station is located, I was aware that they could have parked in the yard of the police station. We were locked up in that van for two or three hours. I don't know exactly how long, but it was close to three hours. It was very hot. I don't know whether they had been in the police station or in a cafe. I had no way of knowing. But they came back, started the van again, and we thought that we were going home. However, they took us to a place which I didn't know exactly what it was. I thought it was some kind of factory. That was Keraterm. And that's where they took us, all three of us. We were asked to produce our identity papers at some sort of reception desk. They took my particulars down and took us inside. There I found some of my neighbours, friends, and that's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. You didn't see any more of Mladjo Radic there, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And my last question: In your opinion, did Mladjo Radic try to help you that day when you were there, when you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes, of course he did, because if he hadn't, he wouldn't have said that it was a mistake and that we were to be taken back home.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And how do you explain the fact that you were not actually taken back home but to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I don't know. It might be that those people who were driving us, who were inside the van, it may be that they thought that Mladjo was not supposed to do something like that, that he could not reverse somebody's orders.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And my last question: In that period, what was Mladjo Radic? Because you were a reserve policeman, you should know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: He was a foot policeman, a policeman on the beat.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is there a rank lower than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: The only thing lower than that was a reserve policeman. That's what I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have promised, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It wasn't even necessary to promise such a thing. So we are going to -- we have been working since 9.30. We need a break. And we should not be in a hurry. Will you please see the witness out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will take a 50-minute break. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Are there any other Defence counsel who wish to put questions to this witness? I see a negative sign of the head on the part of all the counsel. Mr. Saxon, you have the floor for the cross-examination of Witness DC6. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC6, if you can tell me your profession without giving information that will identify yourself. Can you tell me what you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Do you mean now or what I did for a living earlier, in the past?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let's say what you were doing for a living in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I worked as a driver of a rather large vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is your wife a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You described how, on the 4th of June, 1992, you were working as a reserve police officer when your commander called you in and told you that you would have to be relieved of your duties on that day. Did your commander tell you why you were being relieved of your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No, he didn't say why, but from the events which were taking place at the time, it was clear to me, because in the company where I worked before I was dismissed on the 22nd of May without any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say it was clear to you, can you be a little bit more specific? What was clear to you, so the Judges understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: It was clear to me, because on the 22nd of May, when I was discharged, all those who worked in the same company as I did and were of Muslim ethnicity or were Catholic or Croatian, they were all dismissed; they were all fired. And by the same token, in that police station, the majority of my comrades who worked on the reserve police force and were Muslims or Croats had been told, even earlier, that the same thing would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that on the 21st of July, 1992, you were arrested by an active-duty police officer and a reserve police officer. What were the names of these police officers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Is it important for me to say their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we need to go into private session for a moment, perhaps that would be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We shall move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC6, you mentioned that when you were taken to the Omarska camp, Mladjo Radic appeared and asked your escort why you had been brought there, and then the escort showed Mr. Radic some papers. And then you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said that Mladjo Radic took these papers to check. Can you explain what you mean by that? What was Mr. Radic going to check?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I can not explain that because I don't know what was written in those papers. He had a look and returned them to the escorting policeman and who was sitting in the van on the passenger side. He probably looked for the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic say with whom he was going to check, with whom he was going to speak to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear him say anything like that. He only said he was going to inquire whether that was a mistake. Whom he intended to ask, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Radic said -- thank you. I understand your response now. Were you able to see where Mr. Radic went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see where he went because I was inside that van, which had a glass window only on the back, and on the sides there were small windows only. I could only see the upper part of his body through that small window. We were sitting on the floor of the van rather lower than the level of the window, so I couldn't see much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness DC6, did you serve in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From when to when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I do not remember the dates, but it was the winter of 1992, maybe late autumn, until May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you serve -- since you are of Muslim ethnicity and by religion, why did you serve in the Army of the Republika Srpska as opposed to, for instance, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I was born and I lived in the territory of what is now Republika Srpska. All my closer friends came from the ranks of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where did you serve? What places did you serve at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I was in the area of Modrica and the environs, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could have the Court's indulgence for a moment, please? Did you see combat while you were serving in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I have seen it but I haven't participated in any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the units in which you served participate in combat, although perhaps you did not personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the unit that you served in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I don't know the exact name but it was a battalion originating from that area. And since I was a craftsman, if I can call myself that - I was an auto mechanic - I worked on the repair of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you work on the repair of vehicles during the entire time that you served in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally on the frontline and sometimes in the area where I resided, because there was a workshop there where I went to repair vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall the name of the commander of the unit in which you served?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I could not say that, because the commander often changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the court's indulgence, please? Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have only one further question. Re-examined by Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, is it a fact that there were Muslims in the Serbian army as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there a Jovo Divjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I think he was a general. I heard that from the media, from the television.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction, the question was: Were there any Serbs also in the Muslim army, not vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I think there is a problem. Before giving the floor to Mr. Judge Riad, I see that the interpreter says that the question was in fact: Were there also Serbs in the Muslim army, and not vice versa. Mr. Fila, do you have anything to add? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was also does he know the name Jovo Divjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand why the interpreter said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be better for me to repeat this to clarify this completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that is the best way. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs in the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know the name Jovo Divjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes, I know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was he a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was his rank in the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: I don't know what the ranks were in that last war, but I know that the rank of General was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My objection goes to concern for clarity of the record. We have been hearing the term now "Muslim army." I believe the army that is being referred to has a formal name, and perhaps Mr. Fila could ask the witness the name, the formal name of that army, just as I used the name Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Saxon. We are not here for the counsel to testify. The witness said he served in that army, and we cannot put into the witness' mouth the words that you would like to hear. The witness said "Muslim army." That's what I believe I've heard. We cannot put words in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Counsel used the term "Muslim army," Your Honour, and our objection is we don't understand what that means. That's our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official term, I agree, is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it is also true that Republika Srpska is not the so-called Republika Srpska, as Prosecutor Niemann [sic] and the other Prosecutors refer to it. And Republika Srpska has its army. It had it then also, and it was called the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas the Prosecutor refers to it as the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may finish, please. All I want to say is that in all those armies there were people of various ethnicities, and that's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is clear, and what is the problem here finally? I don't see why these questions arise. This has been explained several times. Please, appreciate that we are intelligent people and we all understand it. We are all professionals here, you in the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence counsel. It is not necessary to explain one and the same thing two or three times. From the start, I don't see why we should waste time, so let us finish with this. Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness DC6, good afternoon, if you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... concerning your activities in the police and in the army. You were in the reserve police force till the 4th of June, 1992, till 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then you went to the army from winter 1992 till May 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you said you were dismissed from the police without justification. Were you dismissed to go into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So how did this happen? I mean, you were dismissed from the police. This was for some kind of ethnic reasons or conduct? What was it? Was it because you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I was discharged from the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And if you are discharged from the police force, being a Muslim, would you be accepted in the Army of the Republika Srpska? Is it the same institution, the same policy, or was there a difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite explain the difference between the police force and the army, but I volunteered for the army myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, I have only one question, and it's about your experience in the reserve -- your own experience in the reserve police force before you went to Omarska and Keraterm. You said, when you were describing Mr. Radic as just a foot policeman, you said, "There's nothing lower than that except a reserve policeman," and I just wanted to find out what you meant by that. Did you mean by that that a reserve policeman somehow is underneath or takes orders from or is lower in rank than any active policeman, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: There is no lower rank. A reserve policeman wasn't in fact a lower rank, but as we, as reserve policemen, only worked from time to time, that was our own personal opinion. We considered that active policemen had more experience and -- well, that's what I meant. That was the difference, that they had more experience, whereas we had equal rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to follow up: So that if you were working alongside an active policeman and you were a reserve policeman, could the active policeman give you orders or tell you what to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC6
utterances.text: No. We could work together on the basis of agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Judge Wald. Witness, we have no further questions for you. We thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. Thank you. The usher will now accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From now -- from this time onwards we won't be needing the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that our usher, assistant usher, will be helping us. Our apprentice usher will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next week, we only have one witness with protective measures, coming from America, just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one witness, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought you meant just one witness but one witness with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can you hear me, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a seat. Thank you. Are you sitting comfortably?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming. You are going to start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. -- could you remind me of the name? To be frank, I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Zoran Jovanovic is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the most famous person here, but nonetheless it slipped my mind. Anyway, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: My name is Ranko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: The village of Lamovita, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside now?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Lamovita, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I am a qualified driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your faith?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Serbian, orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, in 1992, the investigations centre or camp was established of Omarska in Omarska. Were any of your friends in the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I have the court's indulgence for a few moments and may we move into private session for the next answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn that they were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mladjo told me that they were there, and I went to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, please, whether you are any relation to Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: We are cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is Mladjo Radic to you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: He is my uncle, my father's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you express the desire to assist those people?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and that is why I went to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I asked Mladjo because at that time he happened to be there. He didn't actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Please continue. What did he actually answer?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: He said that it was forbidden but that in secret I could sort of try and get to them somehow, without anybody knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this assistance distributed to them?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The food I had brought and the personal hygiene items, I gave them to Mladjo and he handed these items to them and they personally confirmed receiving those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember how many times, but I went several other times, taking things. Sometimes in the presence of Mladjo, I would hand them over these things but on many occasions he did this himself, he handed over the items himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the occasions when you yourself handed the items you had brought over --

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mladjo was present there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was Mladjo's behaviour during those occasions?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: He behaved normally. Because he didn't know those friends very well, actually, but he knew they were my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those situations, were you able to talk to anybody else who was present?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I knew some people there who had travelled with me while I worked in the transport business and so I would chat to them about the conditions there, whether they had any problems, and they would tell me that they didn't have any problems but -- and that when Mladjo was in the shift, that he helped them as much as he was able to, to the best of his ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, you said that you are a professional driver. Tell us, please, which company you worked for?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I worked in Autotransport Prijedor as a bus driver and I worked there for about ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know an individual by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew her. (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what are your recollections of that person?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know the degree to which the summaries that are provided to us are supposed to be road maps or not of witness testimony but the summary which I was provided for this witness - who by the way is out of order; we were supposed to have had him after another witness by the same last name - makes no mention of the name (redacted) (redacted)and therefore any preparation for cross has not been done with that in mind, just so the court is aware that we accept in good faith the presentations given to us and -- and at this point, clearly they have gone beyond their own scope. I must make this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you, Ms. Susan Somers, that you were not in the courtroom but how many times - how many times - did the Prosecution step aside from the summaries and how much time have we lost over that here? But we will take note of your objection, Ms. Somers, but I'm also going to give the floor to Mr. Jovanovic. Ms. Susan Somers, this trial -- these proceedings have had a great number of incidents and we wish to arrive at the end of this trial, at the end of this proceeding, these proceedings, and we shall do so. But as I say, we will take note of your objection and I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Jovanovic but I cannot spend time reacting in this way. Mr. Jovanovic, you may respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is a summary in the statement we handed out which implies quotations from the statement, and in one of the paragraphs, it mentions that we shall be discussing this point. I am sorry if the Prosecution has not received this addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Nevertheless, I said what I said. I apologise for saying it in the manner I said it but I did so because the Chamber is always mindful of having -- of giving equal treatment to all parties concerned, and I shall never give that principle up. I am always mindful of treating all the parties in the case equally, on a footing of equality. That's what I wanted to say. And having said that, Mr. Jovanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, Mr. Radic. May we have your recollections with respect to the individual we mentioned, how she behaved at work, at least as far as you yourself were able to note?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, all I can say about this woman is that she was somebody who was not serious. She had problems with disciplinary action in the company because she had appropriated some money, and she worked with tickets and money, and disciplinary action was taken against her. She was irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, and I have one more question. We heard from you that you were engaged in the reserve police force, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can, could you please tell us whether, in the formal competencies that you had once you were engaged in the reserve formations, the reserve police force, did your authority and competence differ in any way from the authority and competence that your cousin Mladjo Radic enjoyed as an active-duty policeman?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: From the time a reserve policeman is activated within the police force, from that moment on he has all the authorisations as the active-duty policeman, as we call him. So once I am mobilised and put on a uniform, from that time on I too am, to all intents and purposes, an active policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I should just like to take advantage of this opportunity to tell you that the Defence of the accused Radic has tendered formal statements which bear out the testimony of this witness here present, and they are formal statements, affidavits, of the witness Dr. Slobodan Savic, Dr. Slobodanka Banovic, Nenad Brkic, and Rade Strika. Thank you, Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jovanovic, but we shall have to consider that question apart. You asked -- the affidavits you mentioned, we will consider them, and we shall hear the opinion of the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask any questions? No, nobody. I see negative signs coming from the Defence counsel. Ms. Susan Somers, your witness for the cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, where did you serve as a reserve policeman, please? Physically, which department, which municipality, which area?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: From the 17th of September, 1991, when I was mobilised and sent to the traffic control section on the road running from Banja Luka to Prijedor in Prijedor municipality. The police station department of Omarska, actually. It's not a police station; it's just this department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One of your obligations would have then been to have restricted the freedom of movement of people coming and going; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. It was my duty to control the traffic, traffic control.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which is movement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. It's the regulation of traffic on the road, to ensure that traffic evolves normally, traffic flows normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that your uncle, the accused Radic, informed you of the presence of two friends of yours, whose names I will not repeat as they were given in closed session, who were found in the Omarska camp. Just to clarify, with no further detail, would you please tell us the ethnicity of these two individuals.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order for you to have access to Omarska camp - which is your testimony, is it not, that you actually went into Omarska camp? - what identification, pass, authorisation, did you obtain, please?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't need them, because many people knew me there; they knew I was a policeman. And those who didn't know me, they asked -- I had to say who I was and why I was going there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, were you a policeman at the Omarska Police Department that your uncle, the accused, was at, that was assigned to handle security at the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were working out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, not in Omarska but on the Prijedor-Banja Luka road, and that is about five kilometres away from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please tell us, who was your commander at the police department physically where you were working? Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: For a time, at the beginning it was Milos Bujic, and later on he was replaced by a man who I think was called Ljuban.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not quite clear. You were a reserve police officer through the Omarska police department, then, the same one that Mladjo Radic was serving at?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you given a tasking at any time to work as a police officer, reserve police officer, in the Omarska investigation centre or camp, as we call it?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So how many times, please, did you go on to the premises of the Omarska camp and talk with or see or be in contact with detainees there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I went three times. Once I talked to some of the people who knew me and whom I knew, but that was just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you please give us the dates on which you went?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I can't. I don't remember. A lot of time has gone by since then, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please: When you went, was Mladjo Radic, the accused, always with you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mostly he was, because I tried to get a bag in to my friends' when he was on duty, because I was afraid that if anybody else was there, they would send me back, wouldn't let me get it through.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So it was Radic's presence that enabled you to get into the camp, your uncle, Mladjo Radic; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Not because of him; because of my friends. But it was surer when he was there. I was more certain of being able to get through and take what I was taking to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So having decided to visit the camp when your uncle, the accused, was there, did he go with you when you came in contact with the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: You mean with those friends of mine? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, with -- I don't know if you limited your contacts to just your friends. It's unclear. You said in your statement: "During these visits I met people I knew who were detained there. I could speak to them, and I asked them about conditions in the centre and their well-being. Some of them asked for cigarettes," et cetera, et cetera. So are these other people besides the two Muslims that you talked about, other people?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were people whom I took cigarettes to. In passing, they would ask me for something, and so when I came back the next time I would bring them the cigarettes or what they had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you knew other people, not just the two Muslims about whom you spoke a bit earlier. I just want to make sure we're clear on that.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, was your uncle, the accused, Radic, with you when you spoke to these individuals about the conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I talked to them alone. It was upon my return, when I would be leaving, after having seen my friends, I would talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then you were free to walk through the camp unescorted, although you were not assigned to that particular location; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it's as you get out of the building where they were, and when I leave that building it meant that I was practically at the end of the camp; I was at the exit to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where was your uncle, the accused, when you were leaving the camp? Did he part ways with you somewhere before that? Was he at his office somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: The office, in the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where was his office, please, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: In that building. I don't know what the building was called. It was the administration building of the mine, and when you go upstairs, on the first floor, on the landing, the right-hand side, was this office, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see the office yourself? Were you there? Did he bring you in there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't go inside, but the door was open and I was outside in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he personally conduct you up there to show you where he worked?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I asked to come into contact with him for me to be able to hand over the food to the friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you came to the camp, were you permitted in before you met your uncle, the accused, or did you have to wait for him to come to the gate to get you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to wait at the gate. I said that people would let me pass because they knew me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you tell your uncle, Mladjo Radic, in advance that you would be coming so that the people you were going to see would be prepared to see you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: While you were talking with various persons about the conditions of the camp, were there other guards or police officers around?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there detainees other than the ones you were talking to around those people? In other words, was it just you and those people alone in a room or were there other people there as well?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was on the way out, when you come out of the building, in front of the building. There were other people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these people with whom you were speaking on the way out?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I know that one of them was called Hase. He worked in my company as a mechanic. There were others, but I really can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you expect to hear anything negative from them?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I expected. They were where they were. Mostly they told me that it wasn't so bad, that it was okay. I don't know much about camps. I was never in one so that I can't really say much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they know that the accused Radic, who was working at Omarska at that time, was your relative?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mladjo?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Some probably knew. I can't say, but I believe that some probably did know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ask them if there was anything you could tell your uncle to make life easier for them on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: He also did what he could to help as much as he could, and that's what I heard from them as well, and I heard that they would say when he was in the shift, that he would help them as much as he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these Muslims, about whom you spoke earlier and whose names we will not discuss, from the same town as you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: They were from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did your uncle, the accused, give you any other names of persons in the camp whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which area of Omarska did you speak to your friends in? What building, please?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: In that building where I went in, the first building that I mentioned. That's where it was. I spoke with them in the corridor and that's where I gave them the things that I had brought for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you could just tell us a description? There are several buildings there, so if you could maybe be a little more specific. When you say the first building, is that the administration building, the hangar? Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think it was the building of the mine where their offices were. I don't know whether that was the administrative building. I never really paid much attention to that because I never went inside when the company was operational. But I think that was a building that belonged to the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: While you were there -- by the way, was it daytime or night-time when you would make these visits, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was in the daytime, the daytime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Every visit was made during the daytime?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the daytime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see any visible signs of injuries on any of the inmates or prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Not on those people that I met with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you heard any sounds that might suggest that people were in pain, screaming, being terrorised?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you find the place to smell? Did you find it fragrant?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was normal for me. It was daytime. The weather was nice. It was normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On any of the occasions when you were in Omarska camp, did you observe any women there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) (redacted) and I asked her about the conditions. I asked her how she was feeling, how it was for her, and then she said everything was okay, that she didn't have any complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see any other women whom you may have known at the camp? Or even if you didn't know them, did you see any other women?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So the only woman you saw was the one whose name you mentioned earlier? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was another woman with her, whom I also knew, and it was just the two of them. Let me just try to remember her name. I think we used to call her Nuska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you would come to visit during the day, was that while you were on duty for your job on the road, the traffic-related job?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, no. I did that in my free time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just one minute, Your Honour. Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic you were born and you live in Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, when you were in the police reserves, was there a section or a station in Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was, and I was transferred to Lamovita because the station was closer to my home. So that's when I was transferred to Lamovita.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander at that department?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Zivko Kos was commander for a while, briefly, and then he was replaced by Prvoslav Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody there by the name of Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Ljuban, Ljuban Grahovac, yes. He also went there with us. He was also a commander. He was a policeman just like we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have two small questions. When you went more than once, you said three times, I think at least, at Omarska camp, you went to the office of your uncle in that administration building, as you said. What kind of office was that? Did he share it with others? Was it a big office? What was the kind of office that was that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't -- I wasn't in the office. I was in the corridor, and the door of the office was open when I got there, and I didn't see any other people there because he had already come out of his office. He had left the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. So you didn't see any other people there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it was his office?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you spoke about (redacted) and Nuska, who were in the camp, the two women. Did you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You saw her and she said no complaint. Did you ask her why she was there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask her but mostly she said she didn't have any complaints about the conditions. Both (redacted) and Nuska told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when you testified, I believe, that when you first saw Mr. Radic and asked him about the possibility of visiting these two friends, he said that visits were forbidden but you could try. My question is: The first time that you tried to make a visit to your friends, did you just show up at the camp or did you get in touch with Mr. Radic first and say, "I'm going to try to come to the camp. Will you be there? Will you meet me?" Did you make any arrangements with him ahead of time before your first visit to the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I set out to enter the camp and then if I was turned back, all right, but in this case, he happened to be there. And when I got to the gate, I said that I would need to go, and if he was there, I would need to go and visit him, and it turned out that he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So just let me make sure I've got it right. The first time -- the first time that you went there, you didn't get in touch with him ahead of time but when you got to the gate, did they let you --

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did they let you get through the gate and then you saw him some place on the camp?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: They knew that he was working but I didn't know and they told me he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So they knew -- the ones at the gate knew that you were somehow connected with him and they told you that he was there, before they let you in or after they let you in, through the first gate?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: The people on the first gate knew both me and him. They knew we were cousins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I wanted to know. My second and last question is: During your three visits, did you see anybody else or hear from other detainees or anyone else about other people besides yourself who didn't work in the camp but were allowed to come and make these visits? Or to your knowledge, are you the only person who was allowed to make these visits if, as your uncle said, they were generally forbidden? Did you know of other people that were allowed to visit their friends or relatives in detention?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Since I went there just very rarely - I was there, as I said three times - I really don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, so it's fair to say you haven't heard -- you didn't hear specifically about -- or see anybody else who didn't work at the camp who was there? Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, we know that you went at least three times to the investigation centre. Did you go at least once without your uncle being there or was he there all the times that you went?

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: He was there all three times when I went because I knew that if he was down there, at least I assumed that they wouldn't turn me back, those three times that I entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you for that answer. We have no further questions. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. We wish you a safe return to your place of residence. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: RANKO RADIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no point in starting another witness. We have two witnesses for tomorrow, Your Honour. They will be brief. And if you planned anything else for tomorrow, we shall have time to go into that as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. Thank you very much. We shall be here again tomorrow. We have some rulings to make. We are going to make the rulings orally. I do not know if the parties would like to discuss anything special tomorrow. Perhaps you could tell us about that, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem and that is the following. The Trial Chamber should decide whether, for the following week, it is necessary for a psychiatrist from Holland - I'm afraid I have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forgotten his name again - Mr. van den Bussche. He said he would be available on Monday or Wednesday but I don't know him personally. So if the Trial Chamber decides tomorrow to bring him in, then somebody will have to do that. As regards the other witness, it is Mr. Beatovic and we suggested that his findings be presented and the cross-examination be conducted in the -- the cross-examination was conducted in the Kunarac case so we need not call him back. Now, I would like to hear your opinions and your decision tomorrow. It would be a little difficult to bring that particular expert back because he lives in Yugoslavia whereas the other one is here at hand. That is the only controversial issue between myself and Ms. Somers. That is all for the moment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there is ever a problem between you and Ms. Somers. That would be impossible, Mr. Fila. But at any rate, I will be responding tomorrow. I apologise, Ms. Susan Somers, I think we ought to lighten the atmosphere a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. I was greeted with a Women's Day greeting earlier so this follows that, I'm sure. Your Honour, I do want to let the Chamber know, because under 94 bis, we did file our objections and we indicated our wish to cross-examine, we will of course seek that cross-examination. I think it's quite important that we do so.
